items.raw_text: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. Microsoft Research at BUILD 2026 Giving developers a hands-on look at some of the many AI-based models and tools they can use to accelerate innovation, enhance their capabilities, and quickly transform ideas into prototypes. Learn more Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. Step 2: A human readable intent map As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Step 3: Proving the login function Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. Step 4: Where proof stops There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification , asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces: The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username . Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. check_password , a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify . It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. generate_token , which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. expiry_from_now , which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. database_error , which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification : /// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) -> (r: Result , sqlx::Error>) ensures // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), { Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body] . Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body: /// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. /// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. /// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; /// that panic is not promised against. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) ensures // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, { ... } Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising. Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising. Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against. Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1. Figure 9. A trust card for check_password . Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them. Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password , written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof. The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. Step 5: Reading the spec The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement. Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions , names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” /// The customers row the database holds for /// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. /// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s /// trusted contract says what it is. pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq ) -> Option ; ... /// What bcrypt says about `password` against a /// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password /// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is /// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. /// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> Option ; /// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> bool { bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) } On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code , since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). /// The account a login names: the customers row for /// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), /// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option , username: Option ) -> Option { match email { Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), None => None, }, None => match username { Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), None => None, }, None => None, }, } } Figure 12. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working. Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: /// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the /// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. /// ... pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, email: Option , username: Option , password: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. email is None && username is None ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) && m@ == missing_identity_text()), // A token only for the account the login names, with its right // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), // The right password for the named account always gets a // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A login naming an account nobody holds gets // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), // The admin role only for an admins row // found by username, with no email sent. (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == admin_role()) ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), // An email login's token always carries the customer role. The Nemotron RL Litmus-Bench V2.0 dataset and benchmark trains and evaluates LLMs and agentic AI models on molecular properties. A practical recipe post-trains Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for scientific use cases by building a custom reinforcement learning environment from experimental data using NeMo Gym and applying RL with NVIDIA NeMo RL. In a drug-metabolism prediction example, supervised fine-tuning improved accuracy by 12% and RL post-training lifted it a further 17% at a 16,384-token output budget. items.title: €9.5 million EU support for fast emergency repair of Baltic Sea submarine cables
items.summary: Today, the European Commission awarded €9.5 million to a pilot project that will develop modular repair capacity for submarine cables in the Baltic Sea. © Christoph Burgstedt The pilot call 'Cable Repair Capacities' was launched in February 2026 as the first of its kind to run under the Digital Global Gateways topic of the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) Digital programme. It aimed to strengthen the emergency response capacity and resilience of backbone network infrastructures by supporting the development and deployment of adaptable repair modules for swift emergency repair operations, enabling a rapid response to incidents that could severely impact the Union or its Member States. Under this call, repair modules are to be hosted in ports or shipyards, from where they can be installed on board ships within a maximum of three days from the vessel's arrival at the port or shipyard. They may be deployed at the request of the Regional Surveillance Hub, as envisaged in the EU Action Plan
items.content: Today, the European Commission awarded €9.5 million to a pilot project that will develop modular repair capacity for submarine cables in the Baltic Sea. © Christoph Burgstedt The pilot call 'Cable Repair Capacities' was launched in February 2026 as the first of its kind to run under the Digital Global Gateways topic of the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) Digital programme. It aimed to strengthen the emergency response capacity and resilience of backbone network infrastructures by supporting the development and deployment of adaptable repair modules for swift emergency repair operations, enabling a rapid response to incidents that could severely impact the Union or its Member States. Under this call, repair modules are to be hosted in ports or shipyards, from where they can be installed on board ships within a maximum of three days from the vessel's arrival at the port or shipyard. They may be deployed at the request of the Regional Surveillance Hub, as envisaged in the EU Action Plan on Cable Security . The selected project, Merikarhu , will ensure the rapid availability of at least one submarine cable repair vessel in the Baltic Sea region, capable of repairing all types of cable damage. In doing so, it will safeguard the continuity of the critical digital and energy infrastructure serving the Member States. This effort contributes to ensuring that Europe's digital infrastructure remains resilient when faced with critical disruptions. Next steps A second call for proposals, 'Submarine Cable Repair Capacities – Works' opened in June 2026 with a budget of €40 million. It funds the same activities as the pilot call but extends the geographical coverage to further sea basins of the Union: the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, including the EU's Outermost Regions, where connectivity relies heavily on submarine cables. This call is open until 25 November 2026 . Related content Press release 05 February 2026 Commission increases submarine cable security with €347 million investment and new toolbox Submarine data cables, carrying 99% of intercontinental internet traffic, are essential for modern life and the European economy. items.content: The PyTorch Foundation is proud to celebrate the winners and nominees of the fourth annual PyTorch Foundation Contributor Awards ! Presented on the keynote stage at PyTorch Conference 2026 in San Jose, California, these awards recognize the individuals whose dedication, innovation, and contributions help advance open source projects and strengthen the communities around them. 2026 Awards at a Glance 15 Award Winners | 11 Nominees | 9 Award Categories | 3 New Categories This year marks another milestone for the program, with 15 award winners, up from 11 in 2025, recognizing outstanding contributions across PyTorch Foundation-hosted projects, including PyTorch, vLLM, Ray, and DeepSpeed. Expanding Recognition Across the PyTorch Ecosystem As the PyTorch Foundation’s community continues to grow, the Contributor Awards have evolved to reflect the diverse ways individuals contribute to its projects. In 2026, three new award categories were introduced: Knowledge Enhancer: Celebrating contributors who make knowledge more accessible through documentation, tutorials, and educational resources. Bug Buster: Recognizing those who identify, report, and resolve bugs that improve project quality and reliability. Catalyst: Honoring contributions that improve developer workflows, automation, infrastructure, and AI-supported development. These additions complement the existing categories recognizing technical innovation, mentorship, community leadership, and ecosystem development. Meet the 2026 Contributor Award Winners Congratulations to our 15 award winners across nine categories! Superhero Thomas Ortner — PyTorch Ecosystem Champion Guangye Yu — PyTorch Knowledge Enhancer Abdulsalam Yazid Bande — PyTorch Suman Debnath — Ray Bug Buster Guilherme Vieira Leobas — PyTorch Vishal Goyal — PyTorch Newcomer Johannes Lennart Zeiser — PyTorch Jiangyun Zhu — vLLM Review Powerhouse Wentao Ye — vLLM Innovator Elfie Guo — PyTorch Masahiro Tanaka — DeepSpeed Xinan Lin — PyTorch Catalyst Harry Mellor — vLLM Jiahao Tan — PyTorch Outstanding Ambassador Jiho Kim — PyTorch Recognizing Our 2026 Award Nominees We also celebrate the 11 award nominees whose contributions and dedication continue to make a difference across the PyTorch ecosystem. Chandra Mohan Singh Negi Arun Bhandari Masahiro Hiramori Luka Govedič Irakli Salia Jiahao Chen Kunshang Ji Rohit Kumar Tiwari Subin George Aaron Gokaslan Xunzhuo Liu Congratulations to all our winners and nominees! Your work helps make the PyTorch ecosystem stronger, more collaborative, and more accessible to developers around the world. Explore the 2026 Contributor Awards and view the honorees Award Ceremony Watch the award ceremony at PyTorch Conference North America. Thank You to Our Community and Sponsor A special thank you to the Contributor Awards Program Committee for the time, care, and thoughtful consideration invested in reviewing nominations and supporting this year’s awards. We also extend our appreciation to Red Hat, sponsor of the 2026 PyTorch Foundation Contributor Awards, for supporting this important community recognition program. And most importantly, thank you to the contributors who continue to build, maintain, document, improve, and champion projects across the PyTorch Foundation ecosystem.

items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful. Grounding in real world signals To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources. O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates. Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions. SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization. Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Validating synthetic quality Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships? Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns? Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics? Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals? End-to-end automation While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases. Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand. Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles. Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels. This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. Spotlight: Microsoft research newsletter Microsoft Research Newsletter Stay connected to the research community at Microsoft. Subscribe today Opens in a new tab Privacy and safety by design Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Results and impact Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments. On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs. On organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure. Conclusion As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety. Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next. At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale . Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets ! items.content: At a glance Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model. Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable. AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. Figure 1. Each finished session teaches TokenEconomizer something about the repository, so later sessions cost less tokens. Where the tokens go We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: Rediscovering the same facts . After a repository had accumulated at least five completed tasks, 30% of tool calls repeated an action from an earlier task in that repository. Only 7% matched an action in another repository’s history. Paying for unused tools . The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called. Getting stuck on failures . The 17% of tasks that failed accounted for 32% of the spending. We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab How TokenEconomizer works After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it. Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use , while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed. Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself. Figure 2. TokenEconomizer works alongside an unchanged coding agent. Micro-skills add learned facts, tool pruning trims the loaded tools, and failure-loop intervention redirects stuck work. Each finished session updates all three. The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls. Saving costs in every repository We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation. Figure 3. On SWE-Bench, TokenEconomizer lowered mean cost per task by 18.4–30.9% across five agent–model combinations (left), while Pass@1 rose in four of them (right). Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction. Figure 4. Cumulative cost change relative to default over each repository’s tasks, using Claude Code. Starting with no history, every repository becomes cheaper by the sixth task. The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower. Looking ahead TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model. The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know. items.content: Data Center / Cloud NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Leads Agentic Inference Performance on MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 Nov 16, 2026 By Zhihan Jiang and Lisa Luh Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary Provisional MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 results show NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers over 10x the throughput per kilowatt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at a shared minimum end-to-end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user. Across Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B models, Vera Rubin NVL72 achieves 5x to 10x higher throughput per kilowatt and 3x to 5x higher end-to-end interactivity at matched concurrency compared with GB300 NVL72. NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, Tensor Cores, and sixth-generation NVLink to support agentic inference demands. Context-aware serving techniques including prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing reduce redundant computation and balance serving load across agentic workloads. Model-specific GPU execution optimizations such as DeepSeek's MegaMoE kernel and Qwen's multi-token prediction with Tensor Core verification reduce data movement and sequential decoding steps. Next Steps Read the companion blog post for more on NVIDIA training and inference performance. Visit MLPerf Endpoints results to review the published benchmark data. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Agentic workloads are demanding more from inference systems. AI agents carry growing conversation histories across turns and generate a mix of reasoning, tool calls, and responses. Inference systems must support users at scale while remaining responsive. MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 evaluates this balance between serving capacity and responsiveness using coding and enterprise workflows through API endpoints. During performance runs, generated tool calls and workflow intent are checked against reference values. Separate SWE-bench Verified evaluations assess end-to-end task-solving capability. These checks evaluate whether faster serving preserves model quality. In MLPerf Endpoints v1.0, provisional NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 results show over 10x the throughput per kilowatt of provisioned power of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at a shared minimum end-to-end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user. 1 This post presents the benchmark results and outlines the hardware and software optimizations used in the submissions. 1 MLPerf® Endpoints v1.0, Kimi K3, Standardized division, Available category, published November 9, 2026. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, 32 accelerators, result 1.0.1.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1p, run 9: concurrency = 1,024 queries, TTFT P90 = 4,673.9 ms, system TPS = 41,414.2 tokens/sec, E2E average interactivity = 50.4 tokens/sec per user, operating power = 100.89 kW. NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, 48 accelerators, result 1.0.0.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1, run 6: concurrency = 48 queries, TTFT P90 = 2,305.1 ms, system TPS = 2,210.4 tokens/sec, E2E average interactivity = 56.2 tokens/sec per user, operating power = 60 kW. Comparison based on throughput per kilowatt at a shared minimum E2E average interactivity of 50 tokens/sec per user. Retrieved from endpoints.mlcommons.org on November 9, 2026. GB300 results verified by MLCommons Association. For the provisional Vera Rubin results: pending MLCommons Association verification, results are subject to change pending peer review. The MLPerf name and logo are registered and unregistered trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. The serving demands of multi-turn agentic AI The MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 dataset captures these workload characteristics: coding trajectories accumulate history over many turns, while enterprise workflows reuse shared instructions, tool definitions, and business rules. Figure 1 shows how context length grows across model responses during extended agentic sessions. Figure 1. Context length grows across model responses in the MLPerf agentic dataset Vera Rubin delivers over 10x the agentic throughput per kilowatt The submissions span Kimi K3, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Table 1 compares provisional Vera Rubin NVL72 results with verified NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 results for throughput per provisioned kilowatt at a shared minimum end-to-end (E2E) interactivity threshold and for E2E interactivity at matched query concurrency. Model Throughput per provisioned kW ratio E2E interactivity ratio Kimi K3 10x 3x DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 9x 5x Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 5x 3x Table 1. Throughput per kilowatt and E2E interactivity ratios for Vera Rubin NVL72 compared with GB300 NVL72² ² MLPerf® Endpoints v1.0, Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Standardized division, Available category. GB300 results published November 4, 2026; Vera Rubin results published November 9, 2026, for Kimi K3 and Qwen, and November 10, 2026, for DeepSeek. Retrieved from endpoints.mlcommons.org on November 10, 2026. Comparisons select each platform’s best TPS/kW meeting the stated minimum E2E average interactivity, or best E2E average interactivity at the stated matched concurrency. Records list: result ID; run number; concurrency (queries); TTFT P90 (ms); System TPS (tokens/sec); E2E average interactivity (tokens/sec per user); operating-point power (kW). DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Throughput/kW at minimum E2E average interactivity 280 tokens/sec per user: Vera Rubin (1.0.1.deepseek-v4_1-flash.mlperf_agentic_inference_dataset.1p; 6; 1,408; 427; 272,711.7; 294.49; 75.67), 24 GPUs; GB300 (1.0.0.deepseek-v4_1-flash.mlperf_agentic_inference_dataset.1; 1; 16; 112.8; 3,054.0; 288.65; 7.50), 4 GPUs. Interactivity at matched concurrency 1,024 queries: Vera Rubin (1.0.1.deepseek-v4_1-flash.mlperf_agentic_inference_dataset.1p; 5; 1,024; 505; 204,207.7; 307.36; 63.06), 20 GPUs; GB300 (1.0.0.deepseek-v4_1-flash.mlperf_agentic_inference_dataset.1; 8; 1,024; 4,073.5; 49,701.8; 56.65; 7.50), 4 GPUs. Interactivity at matched concurrency 256 queries: Vera Rubin (1.0.1.qwen3_6-35b-a3b.agentic_coding.1p; 7; 256; 65.9; 41,142.6; 501.0; 12.61); GB300 (1.0.0.qwen3_6-35b-a3b.agentic_coding.1; 7; 256; 111.7; 23,467.8; 154.5; 7.50). Pending MLCommons Association verification, results are subject to change pending peer review. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. Figure 2 shows the tradeoff between throughput per provisioned kilowatt and E2E interactivity across at least seven concurrency levels per curve. The curves show how much throughput each system delivers at a given responsiveness requirement. The step-function plot does not interpolate between measured points to keep comparisons grounded in demonstrated performance rather than estimates. Figure 2. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 throughput per provisioned kilowatt versus E2E interactivity on Kimi K3 in MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 Higher throughput per kilowatt enables organizations to run more agents simultaneously within the same power budget while meeting the same responsiveness requirement. At low concurrency, faster responses reduce inference wait times for latency-sensitive agentic tasks. Hardware and software optimizations for agentic inference NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, NVIDIA Tensor Cores , and sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink to support the demands of agentic inference. HBM4 enables rapid access to model weights and conversation state, Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations, and NVLink supports communication across GPUs. Context-aware serving and model-specific kernels build on these capabilities to reuse prior work, independently optimize prefill and decode, and accelerate token generation—translating hardware advances into greater inference capacity and faster interactions. Context-aware serving and model-specific optimizations improve inference performance Agentic workloads repeatedly reuse conversation history while adding new instructions and tool results. Efficient serving must preserve reusable state, distribute requests across workers, and accommodate the different execution requirements of prompt processing and token generation. Prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing help reduce redundant computation and balance serving load, while disaggregated serving supports independent optimization of prefill and decode. Figure 3 summarizes how context-aware serving and model-specific GPU execution support agentic inference. Figure 3. Context-aware serving and optimized GPU execution for agentic inference Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B also have distinct architectures that benefit from targeted GPU execution improvements. Model-specific kernels, fusion, optimized memory access, and speculative verification reduce data movement and execution overhead. Table 2 summarizes how these serving and execution techniques work together across the three models. Optimization How it improves performance Context reuse and routing Reuse previously processed conversation state and distribute requests to reduce recomputation and balance worker load. Example: Qwen’s fine-grained prefix matching reuses previously processed history across turns. Prefill and decode optimization Configure prompt processing and token generation independently through disaggregated serving, reducing contention and synchronization waits. Example: Kimi combines disaggregated serving with prefill changes that reduce GPU synchronization waits. Model-specific GPU execution Tailor kernels, fusion, and memory access to each architecture, reducing kernel launches and data movement. Example: DeepSeek’s MegaMoE kernel uses Rubin GPU locality and matrix-multiply instructions. Speculative generation and verification Propose multiple tokens and verify them together, reducing sequential decoding steps. Example: Qwen’s multi-token prediction pairs token proposals with Tensor Core verification. Table 2. Software optimizations improve context reuse, serving efficiency, and GPU execution More productive infrastructure for agentic AI Agentic inference performance depends on co-design across hardware, system architecture, and serving software. The provisional MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 results show how the Vera Rubin platform brings these capabilities together to address the demands of agentic workloads and create more capacity to serve users and scale applications. Learn more about NVIDIA training and inference performance in the companion blog post . Acknowledgements Richard Cai, Viraat Chandra, Xiaoming Chen, Zhenhuan Chen, Alice Cheng, Julien Darve, Ashutosh Dhar, Kefeng Duan, Alec Flowers, Ann Guan, Jie Hao, Rashid Kaleem, Tzu-Ling Kan, Tuhin Khare, Zihao Kong, Jonas Li, Shicheng Li, Yijing Li, Allison Lim, Yanchao Lu, Bofeng Luo, Mingyuan Ma, Matthias Maiterth, Yibai Meng, Stanley Cheong Kwan Phoong, Hanjie Qiu, Zhongdao Ren, Tong Tong, Harshil Vagadia, Lisa Wang, Shang Wang, Xinyu Wang, Fernando Xiong, Yingying Xue, Yuanjing Xue, Lizhi Zhou, and Yaoyang Zhou Discuss (0) Like Tags Agentic AI / Generative AI | Data Center / Cloud | Hardware / Semiconductor | Blackwell | Dynamo | TensorRT-LLM | Intermediate Technical | Benchmark | Blackwell Ultra | GB300 | Groq 3 LPX | InfiniBand | MLPerf | Vera Rubin NVL72 About the Authors About Zhihan Jiang Zhihan Jiang is an engineer manager in the TensorRT team at NVIDIA and focuses on delivering world-class generative AI inference results in MLPerf Inference. Before working on MLPerf, he worked on TensorRT autonomous safety libraries and infrastructure, and NVIDIA CPU architecture modeling. Zhihan holds a master’s degree in Electrical Engineering from Stanford University, and a bachelor’s degree in Computer Engineering from Georgia Tech. View all posts by Zhihan Jiang About Lisa Luh Lisa Luh is a senior technical product marketing manager at NVIDIA, focused on AI inference. Previously, she held product marketing and business development roles at C3 AI and IBM. She holds an MBA from the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration from the Haas School of Business at the University of California, Berkeley. The curves show how much throughput each system delivers at a given responsiveness requirement. The step-function plot does not interpolate between measured points to keep comparisons grounded in demonstrated performance rather than estimates. Figure 2. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 throughput per provisioned kilowatt versus E2E interactivity on Kimi K3 in MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 Higher throughput per kilowatt enables organizations to run more agents simultaneously within the same power budget while meeting the same responsiveness requirement. At low concurrency, faster responses reduce inference wait times for latency-sensitive agentic tasks. Hardware and software optimizations for agentic inference NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, NVIDIA Tensor Cores , and sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink to support the demands of agentic inference. HBM4 enables rapid access to model weights and conversation state, Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations, and NVLink supports communication across GPUs. Context-aware serving and model-specific kernels build on these capabilities to reuse prior work, independently optimize prefill and decode, and accelerate token generation—translating hardware advances into greater inference capacity and faster interactions. Context-aware serving and model-specific optimizations improve inference performance Agentic workloads repeatedly reuse conversation history while adding new instructions and tool results. Efficient serving must preserve reusable state, distribute requests across workers, and accommodate the different execution requirements of prompt processing and token generation. Prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing help reduce redundant computation and balance serving load, while disaggregated serving supports independent optimization of prefill and decode. Figure 3 summarizes how context-aware serving and model-specific GPU execution support agentic inference. Figure 3. Context-aware serving and optimized GPU execution for agentic inference Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B also have distinct architectures that benefit from targeted GPU execution improvements. Model-specific kernels, fusion, optimized memory access, and speculative verification reduce data movement and execution overhead. Table 2 summarizes how these serving and execution techniques work together across the three models. Optimization How it improves performance Context reuse and routing Reuse previously processed conversation state and distribute requests to reduce recomputation and balance worker load. Example: Qwen’s fine-grained prefix matching reuses previously processed history across turns. Prefill and decode optimization Configure prompt processing and token generation independently through disaggregated serving, reducing contention and synchronization waits. Example: Kimi combines disaggregated serving with prefill changes that reduce GPU synchronization waits. Model-specific GPU execution Tailor kernels, fusion, and memory access to each architecture, reducing kernel launches and data movement. Example: DeepSeek’s MegaMoE kernel uses Rubin GPU locality and matrix-multiply instructions. Speculative generation and verification Propose multiple tokens and verify them together, reducing sequential decoding steps. Example: Qwen’s multi-token prediction pairs token proposals with Tensor Core verification. Table 2. Software optimizations improve context reuse, serving efficiency, and GPU execution More productive infrastructure for agentic AI Agentic inference performance depends on co-design across hardware, system architecture, and serving software. The provisional MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 results show how the Vera Rubin platform brings these capabilities together to address the demands of agentic workloads and create more capacity to serve users and scale applications. Learn more about NVIDIA training and inference performance in the companion blog post . items.content: Data Center / Cloud NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Achieves up to 2x Blackwell Ultra Performance in MLPerf Training v6.1 Nov 16, 2026 By Farshad Ghodsian and Sukru Burc Eryilmaz Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 debuted in MLPerf Training v6.1 and delivered the fastest time to train on six of seven benchmarks, achieving up to 2x more performance per GPU than an optimized GB300 NVL72 baseline. On the DeepSeek-V3 671B Mixture-of-Experts benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the model in 4.14 minutes using 1,024 GPUs, halving the 8.03-minute time of GB300 NVL72 at the same scale. Vera Rubin NVL72 also led the new Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO reinforcement learning post-training benchmark with a 10.44-minute result at 1,024 GPUs, and demonstrated software maturity by submitting with both TensorRT-LLM and vLLM inference backends. The platform maintained above 97% scaling efficiency when expanding from 256 to 1,024 GPUs on DeepSeek-V3, enabled by a copper NVLink 6 spine delivering 3.6 TB/s per GPU and ConnectX-9 SuperNICs over Quantum-X800 InfiniBand or Spectrum-X Ethernet. Unverified reruns with a newer software stack further reduced Vera Rubin NVL72 time to train on Llama 3.1 8B, gpt-oss 20B, and DLRMv4, demonstrating continuous optimization after hardware ships. Eighty percent of closed-division submissions ran on NVIDIA platforms across 20 partner organizations, and Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are generally available through cloud infrastructure partners worldwide. Next Steps Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform for AI training and inference. See the full MLPerf Training v6.1 results for detailed benchmark data. Read the MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 blog to see how Vera Rubin leads in agentic inference. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more As AI agents tackle increasingly complex workflows, reducing time-to-train is critical for rapidly iterating on both models and the agents they power. MLPerf Training v6.1 marks the debut of the NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture, and these early results demonstrate that its CUDA software stack is already highly mature. In its first appearance, the Vera Rubin NVL72 platform delivered the fastest time to train on six of the seven benchmarks, achieving up to 2x more performance than a highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 baseline. For the seventh benchmark, DeepSeek-V3 671B, NVIDIA captured the absolute fastest time of the round by demonstrating massive scale on a 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster. This dual-platform approach deliberately showcases the strengths of both systems. While the GB300 results highlight the massive, reliable cluster scale NVIDIA is deploying today, Vera Rubin demonstrated its own exceptional scaling architecture by maintaining above 97% overall efficiency when scaling from 256 to 1,024 GPUs. Together, NVIDIA platforms hold the fastest time to train on every benchmark in v6.1. NVIDIA platforms were also the only ones to submit results across all seven benchmarks, with Vera Rubin successfully completing the entire suite in its inaugural run. For developers, this breadth matters as much as any single top-line number. It proves that the performance gains inherited on day one span the entire modeling pipeline, comprehensively supporting everything from large-scale pretraining to the reinforcement learning post-training required for modern AI agents. Comprehensive AI performance across all MLPerf training benchmarks The simplest way to read this round is per benchmark: How much more performance does the new platform deliver per GPU on the same model? Model type Benchmark GPU Count Vera Rubin NVL72 vs. optimized GB300 NVL72 Submission ID (Vera Rubin / GB300) Mixture-of-Experts DeepSeek-V3 671B 1,024 2x 6.1-0116 / 6.1-0030 Mixture-of-Experts Qwen3.5 397B GRPO (RL) 64 1.4x 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0020 Mixture-of-Experts gpt-oss 20B 64 1.6x 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0049 Dense Llama 2 70B LoRA 72 1.5x 6.1-0123 / 6.1-0138 Dense Llama 3.1 8B 72 1.6x 6.1-0073 / 6.1-0138 Diffusion FLUX.1 72 1.5x 6.1-0124 / 6.1-0138 Recommender DLRMv4 128 1.4x 6.1-0129 / 6.1-0038 Table 1. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. Figure 1. Vera Rubin NVL72 performance relative to GB300 NVL72 at the same GPU count on all seven MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmarks MLPerfTraining v6.1 results retrieved from www.mlcommons.org on Nov 16, 2026, from the following entries: 6.1-0116 , 6.1-0030, 6.1-0135, 6.1-0020, 6.1-0049, 6.1-0123, 6.1-0138, 6.1-0073, 6.1-0124, 6.1-0129 and 6.1-0038. The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. The pattern is clear. The largest gain lands on the largest, most communication-heavy model. While the platform is consistently 1.4x to 1.6x faster across the rest of the suite, the generational advantage widens even further for the massive DeepSeek-V3 benchmark. The suite covers natural language, image generation, recommendation, and reinforcement learning, so the gains hold across multiple modalities as well as across different model shapes and architectures. DeepSeek-V3 671B: 2x per GPU on the hardest workload DeepSeek-V3 671B is a 671-billion-parameter token-dropless Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model and the most demanding workload in the suite. Expert parallelism turns every iteration into a burst of all-to-all communication, so fabric efficiency shows up directly in time to train. Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the benchmark in 4.14 minutes using 1,024 GPUs across 16 racks. GB300 NVL72 ran the identical 1,024-GPU configuration in 8.03 minutes, close to 2x per GPU, and the largest generational improvement in this round. Halving time to train roughly doubles how many experiments a team can run in a quarter, and experiment throughput is what moves model quality. At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result of the round: 1.38 minutes across 10,240 GPUs. That is one training job spread across 160 racks, each its own NVLink domain, and it shows the platform’s scale-out fabric holding up long after the job outgrows a single rack. Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark , Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO, reflecting a fundamental shift in AI development. Post-training has emerged as the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, making the GRPO workload uniquely demanding. The continuous cycle of generating rollouts, scoring them, and updating weights pushes system architectures to their limits by forcing constant, massive weight migrations between inference and training engines. Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved the fastest time for this new benchmark with a time of 10.44 minutes at 1,024 GPUs (6.1-0117), compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72 (6.1-0031) at the same scale. The Vera Rubin platform also proved its flexibility by submitting on two different inference backends: NVIDIA NeMo RL with TensorRT-LLM at 10.44 minutes and with vLLM at 10.94 minutes (6.1-0118). Shipping two viable inference backends on a benchmark this new says as much about software maturity as it does about silicon. Teaching these models to observe, reason, and act requires running each rollout in a simulated environment and executing tool calls, code, or API validations. Because driving these simulations is intensely CPU-bound, the NVIDIA Vera CPU is integral to the architecture , sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments across 256 CPUs in a single Vera CPU rack. While the GPUs handle massive token generation and rapid weight updates, the Vera CPUs work in lockstep to simulate the environments, ensuring the accelerators are continuously fed with the rich feedback required to perfect agentic workflows. NVLink, Quantum-X and Spectrum-X: Co-designed networking for high-efficiency AI scaling Every result above is also a networking result. Modern AI training requires thousands of processors to act as one, a challenge NVIDIA solves by co-designing the internal rack domain and the external cluster fabric. Inside the rack, Vera Rubin NVL72 connects 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs through a copper NVLink 6 spine. Delivering 3.6 TB/s per GPU and 260 TB/s per rack, this all-to-all domain keeps MoE expert dispatch off the critical path. Beyond the rack, the platform scales out via ConnectX-9 SuperNICs over Quantum-X800 InfiniBand or Spectrum-X Ethernet. To manage bursty MoE traffic, both fabrics use adaptive routing and congestion control to keep all-to-all communications hidden behind the compute layer. This cohesive design translates directly to efficiency. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved above 97% scaling efficiency as it scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs (4 to 16 racks). GB300 NVL72 showcased the platform’s large-scale capabilities , extending to 10,240 GPUs to capture the fastest absolute result of the round. Because the NVL72 architecture provides a consistent 72-GPU domain, developers see predictable performance jumps every generation without altering their operating model. Each cycle simply delivers more compute and bandwidth across the same consistent fabric. Figure 2. Three generations of NVL72 systems at an identical 1,024-GPU scale MLPerfTraining v6.1 results retrieved from www.mlcommons.org on Nov 16, 2026, from the following entries: 6.1-0045, 6.1-0030 and 6.1-0116. Ratios are rounded. The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. Continuous software optimization: Unlocking faster pretraining without hardware upgrades Vera Rubin’s results came from the NVIDIA AI software stack that customers receive: NVIDIA NeMo Framework 26.09 for the pretraining benchmarks, NVIDIA NeMo RL for the reinforcement learning benchmark, and NVIDIA PyTorch releases for FLUX.1 and DLRMv4. The optimizations are the ones described in our MLPerf Training v6.0 round . The stack also keeps moving after a round closes. Since v6.1 submissions were finalized, we have re-run several of the benchmarks on the same hardware and configuration with a newer software build. These are unverified results rather than MLCommons submissions, and we are sharing them because they show how continuous optimizations make NVIDIA infrastructure highly productive, durable, and fungible. Ratios are rounded. Unverified results have not been verified by MLCommons Association. Unverified results have not been through an MLPerf review and may use measurement methodologies and/or workload implementations that are inconsistent with the MLPerf specification for verified results. The MLPerf name and logo are registered and unregistered trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. That is what a mature software stack means for customers. The infrastructure gets faster after it ships, and the improvements continue to arrive, extending the platform’s productive lifetime and revenue generating potential. Because the CUDA platform is highly programmable, customers can unlock even more performance on their own. For example, Thinking Machines Lab developed an NVFP4 training recipe and custom kernels for its Inkling 2 Small model on GB300 NVL72, using NVFP4 for forward-pass MoE GEMMs and MXFP8 for gradients. Compared with full MXFP8 training, it sped up pretraining and fine-tuning by 8% and reinforcement learning by 20%, with minimal accuracy impact. An ecosystem that shipped on day one Vera Rubin’s debut in MLPerf Training v6.1 proves the architecture is built for immediate global deployment. With 80 percent of all closed-division submissions running on NVIDIA platforms across 20 partner organizations, these benchmarks represent reproducible performance across clouds and OEMs rather than isolated laboratory peaks. Systems are already generally available across various cloud infrastructure partners, complementing a multitude of AI Factory deployments around the globe. Today, Vera Rubin leads on performance per GPU across all seven workloads, while Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra maintain the scale record. Azure’s 2,560-node, 10,240-GPU GB200 NVL72 submission tied the NVIDIA 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 run to claim this round’s largest clusters. Partners are also pushing the limits of the architecture at the node level: Firmus used AI-driven kernel generation, with automated performance testing and mathematical validation, to post the fastest GB300 8-GPU result of the round, training GPT-OSS 20B in 52.90 minutes (6.1-0091) and Llama 3.1 8B in 52.40 minutes (6.1-0094). Because these platforms share a continuously optimizing CUDA software stack, developers can expect these inaugural metrics to climb steadily higher before the next MLPerf round even begins. As the Vera Rubin software stack matures the way the Blackwell stack did, expect these initial performance advantages to continue to unlock even greater value throughout the platform’s lifecycle. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform and see the full MLPerf Training v6.1 results or read our MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 blog to see how Vera Rubin leads the industry in agentic inference.
